\title{The Union Wage Effect Revisited:\\Registry Evidence from Three Decades}
\author{H.~Bergstr\"om and T.~A.~Mwikali}
\date{February 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We revisit the classical question of how much union members earn above
comparable non-members using population registry data covering 1991 to
2022. Our baseline estimate of the union wage premium is 11.2 percent,
with substantial heterogeneity across cohorts and sectors. The premium
has compressed over time in the private sector but remained stable in the
public sector, and we show that most of the compression is explained by
the declining selectivity of union membership rather than by weaker
bargaining outcomes.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Few questions in labour economics have attracted as much empirical
attention as the size and interpretation of the wage premium associated
with union membership. Early cross-sectional studies routinely reported
an earnings premium of 15 to 25 percent, while panel estimates that
control for worker fixed effects typically found values less than half as
large. The divergence between these literatures is still not fully
understood, and it matters for how policy makers interpret the decline of
collective bargaining coverage across the OECD.

This paper brings new evidence to the question using administrative
earnings records linked to employer reports of bargaining coverage and
union membership status. The registry setting gives us three advantages
over the survey-based literature: sample sizes in the millions, exact
measurement of membership status rather than self-reports, and a long
panel that lets us track the same workers through spells of membership
and non-membership. We can therefore estimate the pay premium within
workers over time, and we can ask how the premium has evolved as
membership itself has become less common and less selective.

The literature has long debated whether an earnings premium estimated
from cross-sectional comparisons can be given a causal reading. Studies
based on skill-matched comparisons tend to report larger earnings
premiums than studies that follow the same worker over time, and the
gap between the two approaches is usually attributed to unobserved
ability. Our registry design lets us quantify this attribution directly,
because the within-worker pay premium and the cross-sectional gap can be
estimated on identical samples and reconciled through decompositions.

Our headline findings are as follows. The pooled cross-sectional wage
premium averages 16.4 percent over the full period, but the within-worker
estimate is 11.2 percent, implying that about a third of the raw gap
reflects selection on persistent worker characteristics. The within-worker
earnings premium fell from 13.8 percent in the 1990s to 9.6 percent in
the 2010s in the private sector, while remaining essentially flat in the
public sector. Decompositions show that the decline is accounted for by
changing selection: as membership contracted, the workers who remained
members became less negatively selected, which mechanically raised the
cross-sectional gap even as the causal wage premium compressed.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes the
institutional setting. Section 3 presents the registry data. Section 4
lays out the empirical strategy. Section 5 reports the main estimates,
Section 6 explores heterogeneity, Section 7 examines mechanisms, and
Section 8 collects robustness checks. Section 9 concludes.

\section{Institutional Background}
Collective agreements in the setting we study are negotiated primarily at
the sector level, with firm-level supplements in larger establishments.
Membership in a union is voluntary and portable across employers, and
dues are partially tax deductible. Bargaining coverage extends to many
non-members through extension provisions, which complicates the
interpretation of any measured earnings premium: covered non-members may
enjoy the same negotiated schedules even though they do not pay dues.

Two features of the period matter for our analysis. First, membership
density fell from 57 percent in 1991 to 38 percent in 2022, with the
decline concentrated among younger workers and in private services.
Second, the share of workers covered by sector agreements fell much less,
from 71 to 66 percent, so that the gap between membership and coverage
widened. This divergence makes our setting particularly informative about
what the pay premium actually captures, since the institutional channel
through which membership maps into pay weakened over time.

\section{Data}
Our data combine the central population register, the employee--employer
register, and the tax records for the universe of workers aged 20 to 60
between 1991 and 2022. Union membership is observed from the deduction of
dues in the tax records, which the tax authority validates against union
registers. Annual earnings are measured as total taxable labour income,
and hourly wages are available for the subset of workers in firms that
report contractual hours to the employer register.

The analysis sample excludes the self-employed, workers with fewer than
six months of employment in a year, and workers in agriculture and the
armed forces. The final panel contains 4.1 million workers and 61 million
person-year observations. We deflate all nominal amounts to 2015 prices
using the consumer price index, and we winsorise earnings at the top and
bottom half percent of each year's distribution.

Descriptive statistics document the raw gaps that motivate the analysis.
Members earn more than non-members in every year of the sample, but the
raw earnings premium widens after 2005 even as membership falls, a
pattern that foreshadows the selection story told by the decompositions.
Members are older, more likely to work in manufacturing and the public
sector, and more likely to have completed vocational secondary education.
Because the raw earnings premium varies so much with age and sector, all
descriptive gaps reported below are residualised on these observables
before being compared with the regression estimates.

\section{Empirical Strategy}
Our baseline specification regresses log annual earnings on an indicator
for union membership, with year fixed effects and a rich set of worker
and job controls. To isolate the within-worker component of the wage
premium we add worker fixed effects, so that identification comes from
the roughly 900 thousand workers who switch membership status at least
once during the panel. We cluster standard errors at the worker level and
report specification checks with firm fixed effects and with
sector-by-year fixed effects.

The identifying assumption is that switches of membership status are not
timed to transitory earnings shocks. Two features of the data support
this assumption. Event studies around switches show flat pre-trends in
earnings for three years before the switch, and the estimated premium is
nearly identical when we exclude workers who change employer in the same
year as the switch, suggesting that job mobility does not confound the
estimates. We also instrument membership with the sector-level density in
the worker's first job, following the logic that early exposure shifts
the propensity to join without directly affecting later earnings.

\section{Main Results}
Table 1 reports the baseline estimates. The pooled cross-sectional wage
premium is 16.4 percent with a standard error of 0.2 percent. Adding
worker fixed effects reduces the estimate to 11.2 percent, and the
further addition of firm fixed effects leaves it essentially unchanged at
10.9 percent. The instrumented within-worker estimate is 12.6 percent,
somewhat above the fixed-effects estimate, consistent with negative
selection into membership among switchers.

Splitting the sample by period shows that the pay premium has compressed
in the private sector, from 13.8 percent in the 1991--2000 window to
9.6 percent in 2011--2022, while the public-sector estimate moves from
8.4 to 8.1 percent, an insignificant change. The contrast between the
sectors is one of the central facts of the paper, and it is robust to
alternative sample definitions and to measuring earnings at the hourly
rather than the annual frequency.

The earnings premium estimated on hourly wages is consistently about one
percentage point smaller than the annual estimate, indicating that a
minor part of the annual gap reflects differences in hours worked rather
than in rates of pay. All subsequent results use annual earnings unless
otherwise noted, since the hours data are missing for a substantial
minority of worker-years.

\section{Heterogeneity}
The wage premium varies systematically across workers. It is largest for
workers with vocational secondary education, at 13.9 percent, and
smallest for university graduates, at 6.8 percent. It is larger for women
than for men by about two percentage points, and it declines with
experience over the first half of the career before flattening. These
patterns align with the view that collective bargaining compresses the
returns to observable skills, so that the groups with the lowest
bargaining power individually gain the most from membership.

Sectoral detail reveals further structure. The premium is negative and
significant in financial services, small and insignificant in
professional services, and largest in transportation and in
manufacturing. The cross-sector ranking is stable over time even as the
average level compresses, which suggests that sector-level bargaining
institutions, rather than sectoral composition shifts, drive the level
differences we document.

Cohort analysis shows that the earnings premium for workers who entered
the labour market after 2000 is about three percentage points below the
premium for earlier cohorts at the same age, and that this cohort gap
widens as cohorts age. Combined with the sectoral results, this pattern
points to a slow erosion of the bargaining channel in exactly those parts
of the economy where membership has become least common.

\section{Mechanisms}
We consider three candidate mechanisms for the documented compression.
The first is declining bargaining power, under which the causal effect of
membership on negotiated pay falls over time. The second is changing
selection, under which the composition of members shifts in a way that
alters the measured wage premium even if the causal effect is constant.
The third is the widening coverage gap, under which extension provisions
deliver negotiated schedules to a growing share of non-members and
thereby shrink the measured gap between members and non-members.

A Kitagawa--Oaxaca--Blinder decomposition of the change in the
cross-sectional gap assigns more than two thirds of the change to
composition, leaving at most one third to a changing structure of pay.
The fixed-effects estimates, which are immune to time-invariant
composition, show a decline of about four percentage points in the
private sector, and we attribute this residual decline primarily to the
coverage channel. Direct evidence for the coverage channel comes from
covered non-members, whose earnings premium relative to uncovered
non-members rose over the same period.

Earnings premium estimates that ignore the coverage margin will, in this
setting, understate the reach of collective bargaining, because they
compare members with a control group that increasingly shares the same
negotiated schedules. An earnings premium computed against genuinely
uncovered workers is correspondingly larger and declines less steeply.

The mechanism analysis therefore reconciles the two stylised facts that
motivated the paper: a widening raw gap alongside a shrinking causal
premium is exactly what one expects when a once broadly representative
institution contracts into a smaller, more positively selected core while
its negotiated schedules continue to cover a large fringe of non-members.

\section{Robustness}
The results are robust to a long list of specification checks. Estimates
are stable when we restrict the sample to job stayers, when we measure
membership at the monthly frequency, when we trim the earnings
distribution more aggressively, and when we reweight the sample to hold
the age and education composition constant at its 1991 distribution. The
event-study estimates show no evidence of anticipation effects, and the
premium estimated off switches that coincide with a change of sector is
similar to the baseline. Pay premium estimates obtained from the hourly
wage subsample track the annual estimates closely in every period, and
the pay premium measured on contracted rather than actual hours differs
by less than half a percentage point from the baseline.

\section{Conclusion}
Using three decades of population registry data, we have shown that the
union wage premium remains economically meaningful but is smaller than
the raw gap suggests, and that its evolution over time is dominated by
selection rather than by a collapse of bargaining outcomes. For policy,
the results caution against reading the decline of membership as evidence
that collective bargaining has become irrelevant to pay determination:
the coverage of negotiated schedules remains broad, and the premium for
covered workers has been resilient. Future work will extend the analysis
to non-wage outcomes, including hours stability, layoff risk, and access
to training, where the role of membership may be larger than it is in the
pay dimension studied here.
\end{document}
